Rivers are the arteries of the land, carrying water from mountain snowfields and hidden springs down to the sea. They start as small trickles, collecting rain and meltwater, and grow as tributaries join them. Along the way they carve valleys, cut canyons through solid rock, and build fertile floodplains from the sediment they carry. The Nile, the Amazon, the Yangtze and the Mississippi each drain huge basins, moving enormous volumes of water and soil every year. A river is never really the same from one moment to the next. Its channel shifts, its banks wear away, and its flow rises and falls with the seasons.

People have always settled beside rivers. Early civilizations grew along the Tigris, Euphrates, Indus and Nile, where reliable water and rich silt made farming possible. Rivers became highways for trade, borders between nations, and sources of power for mills and, later, hydroelectric dams. They also support a huge range of life, from fish and insects to the forests and wetlands along their edges. Today many rivers face pollution, over-extraction and damming, which threaten both ecosystems and the communities that depend on them. Protecting rivers means protecting the living systems that have shaped human history.
